Libraries

library(fpp3)

The ETS statistical framework and model selection

Minimizing the SSE vs maximizing the likelihood

Writing exponential smoothing as a statistical model (fpp3 8.5) makes it possible to compute the likelihood of a model: how probable the observed data are if that model generated them. The likelihood is a joint probability density, evaluated at the data. A larger likelihood means a model that fits the data better. The handwritten primer 19_A_MLE_Informal_Intro.pdf in this folder builds the idea from the normal distribution.

  • For an additive error model, maximizing the likelihood (assuming normally distributed errors) gives the same parameters as minimizing the sum of squared errors, which is what Sessions 15 to 18 did.
  • For a multiplicative error model, the two give different results. Maximizing the likelihood is what ETS() does in both cases.

Information criteria vs the likelihood

Information criteria combine the likelihood with a penalty for the number of parameters. Maximizing the likelihood alone always favors the model with more parameters, because extra parameters can only help the fit to the training data. The penalty compensates for that, and protects against overfitting.

Information criteria vs cross-validation

The information criteria used here are \(AIC\), \(AIC_c\) and \(BIC\). Because they are built on the likelihood, they can only compare models of the same class, fitted to the same response variable (after any transformation). They can choose an ETS model among ETS models; they cannot compare an ETS model with a model of another class, such as the ARIMA models of the follow-up course, whose likelihood is computed differently. They also cannot compare a model of y with a model of log(y).

To compare models of different classes, or of differently transformed data, use cross-validation (Session 14).

The information criteria

AIC: Akaike’s Information Criterion

For ETS models:

\[ \text{AIC} = -2\log(L) + 2k \]

  • \(L\) is the likelihood of the model.
  • \(k\) is the total number of parameters and initial states that have been estimated, including the residual variance. It measures the complexity of the model.

The lower the AIC, the better. The first term falls as the fit improves; the second rises with every parameter.

AICc: the bias-corrected AIC

For small samples (small \(T\), the length of the series), the AIC tends to choose models with too many parameters. The corrected version works better:

\[ \text{AIC}_{\text{c}} = \text{AIC} + \frac{2k(k+1)}{T-k-1} \]

As with the AIC, lower is better. ETS() uses the \(AIC_c\) by default when it chooses a model.

BIC: the Bayesian Information Criterion

\[ \text{BIC} = \text{AIC} + k[\log(T)-2] \]

The BIC penalizes each parameter more heavily than the AIC once \(T\) is 8 or more (\(\log T > 2\)), so it chooses either the same model as the AIC or one with fewer parameters.

Model combinations that are excluded

Three combinations of (Error, Trend, Season) can be numerically unstable, because their state equations divide by values that may be close to zero:

  • \(ETS(A, N, M)\)
  • \(ETS(A, A, M)\)
  • \(ETS(A, Ad, M)\)

They are not considered when ETS() chooses a model. With trends N, A and Ad, errors A and M, and seasons N, A and M, that leaves 15 of the 18 combinations.

Models with multiplicative errors

  • Useful when the data are strictly positive.
  • Numerically unstable when the data contain zeros or negative values, so ETS() does not consider multiplicative errors for a series that is not strictly positive.

Session 11’s transformations, such as \(\log(1+x)\) for data with zeros, are one way around this. Remember that a transformation changes the interpretation of the model and the shape of the forecast distribution, as Session 12 showed.

Residuals and multiplicative errors

With multiplicative errors, the residuals and the innovation residuals differ, even without a transformation. augment() returns both:

  • Response residuals (.resid): \(\hat{e}_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\).
  • Innovation residuals (.innov):
    • additive error model: \(\hat{\varepsilon}_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\);
    • multiplicative error model: \(\hat{\varepsilon}_t = \dfrac{y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}}{\hat{y}_{t|t-1}}\), a relative error.

So for a multiplicative error model, run Session 9’s residual diagnostics on .innov, which is the error the model assumes to be white noise.

Automatic ETS model selection

How to ask ETS() to choose

When the formula does not fix a component, ETS() tries every allowed option for it and keeps the model with the lowest \(AIC_c\). With no specials at all, ETS(y), it searches all 15 combinations.

Example 1: national populations

Automatic models for the population of every country in global_economy. One country has missing values, which ETS() does not accept, so it raises a warning and fits nothing for that country.

fit <- global_economy |>
  mutate(Pop = Population / 1e6) |>
  model(ets = ETS(Pop))

fit
# A mable: 263 x 2
# Key:     Country [263]
   Country                      ets
   <fct>                    <model>

 2 Albania             <ETS(M,A,N)>

 5 Andorra             <ETS(M,A,N)>
 6 Angola              <ETS(M,A,N)>
 7 Antigua and Barbuda <ETS(M,A,N)>
 8 Arab World          <ETS(M,A,N)>
 9 Argentina           <ETS(A,A,N)>
10 Armenia             <ETS(M,A,N)>

The AIC can be rebuilt from the log-likelihood. China’s model has four parameters and initial states, plus the residual variance, so \(k = 5\):

log_lik <- fit |> glance() |> filter(Country == "China") |> pull(log_lik)

# k = 4 parameters and initial states + 1 residual variance
-2 * log_lik + 2 * (4 + 1)
[1] 395.7744
fit |> glance() |> filter(Country == "China") |> pull(AIC)
[1] 395.7744

fit |>

  autoplot()

Forecasting with ETS models

The fitted model gives point forecasts and prediction intervals with forecast(), as for every model in the course (fpp3 8.7). Australian domestic holiday trips:

aus_holidays <- tourism |>
  filter(Purpose == "Holiday") |>
  summarise(Trips = sum(Trips) / 1e3)

fit <- aus_holidays |>
  model(ETS(Trips))

report(fit)
Series: Trips 
Model: ETS(M,N,A) 
  Smoothing parameters:
    alpha = 0.3484054 
    gamma = 0.0001000018 

  Initial states:
     l[0]       s[0]      s[-1]      s[-2]    s[-3]
 9.727072 -0.5376106 -0.6884343 -0.2933663 1.519411

  sigma^2:  0.0022

     AIC     AICc      BIC 
226.2289 227.7845 242.9031

ETS() chose \(ETS(M,N,A)\): multiplicative errors, no trend, additive seasonality. It was a close call:

aus_holidays |>
  model(
    MNA = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("N") + season("A")),
    MNM = ETS(Trips ~ error("M") + trend("N") + season("M"))
  ) |>
  glance() |>
  select(.model, AICc)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  .model  AICc
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 MNA     228.
2 MNM     228.

The two seasonal forms are within a fraction of a point of \(AIC_c\), and measured in thousands of trips instead of millions (Exercise 2) the choice flips to \(ETS(M,N,M)\). When two models are that close, the criterion cannot tell them apart, and either is defensible.

fit |>
  forecast(h = 8) |>
  autoplot(aus_holidays) +
  labs(title = "Australian domestic tourism",
       y = "Overnight trips (millions)")

Three points about these forecasts:

  • Point forecasts. ETS point forecasts are the means of the forecast distributions, except for models with multiplicative seasonality. This model has additive seasonality, so .mean is the mean.
  • Intervals. The prediction intervals differ between models with additive and multiplicative components: with multiplicative errors they widen with the level of the series.
  • How they are computed. For some ETS models there is no formula for the forecast variance. Then forecast() simulates many future paths and takes percentiles of them, the bootstrap idea from Session 12, with simulated errors.
fit |>
  forecast(h = 8) |>
  hilo(level = 95) |>
  head(4)
# A tsibble: 4 x 5 [1Q]
# Key:       .model [1]
  .model     Quarter
  <chr>        <qtr>
1 ETS(Trips) 2018 Q1
2 ETS(Trips) 2018 Q2
3 ETS(Trips) 2018 Q3
4 ETS(Trips) 2018 Q4
# ℹ 3 more variables: Trips <dist>, .mean <dbl>, `95%` <hilo>
